analysis.one_liner: Expands and fixes the public service student loan forgiveness program so teachers, nurses, and other public servants can qualify.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 83 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrote the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which cancels federal student loans for people who work in government or nonprofits. It would have forgiven half a borrower's loans after five years of public service payments instead of making them wait ten years for full forgiveness, counted older bank-based federal loans for the first time, fixed rules that wipe out credit when loans are consolidated, and forced the Education Department to tell borrowers where they stand. The bill never moved after being sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Public service workers with federal student debt: teachers, nurses, first responders, social workers, public defenders and prosecutors, librarians, and early childhood and military-service workers. Borrowers with older FFEL loans, who were previously shut out of the program entirely, would have become eligible. Current participants would have gotten credit for past payments and retroactive partial forgiveness.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public servants with federal student loans

how_it_helps.text: A borrower who makes 60 qualifying monthly payments while working full-time for a government or qualifying nonprofit would have 50% of their loan balance forgiven, with full forgiveness at 120 payments; full-time is defined as 30 hours a week, including across two jobs [S3].

Borrowers with loans under the Federal Family Education Loan program would become eligible for public service loan forgiveness, and past payments made on component loans would count when loans are consolidated, instead of being erased as they were under the old rules [S2, S3].

Borrowers in deferment or forbearance could later make payments to satisfy up to 36 past monthly obligations, and the Education Department would have to notify borrowers at least twice a year how many qualifying payments they have made and how many remain [S3].

The bill requires a dispute resolution process for contested payment counts, a database of qualifying employers, data-matching with federal agencies so borrowers do not have to certify employment repeatedly, and protections against retroactive decisions that strip already-credited payments [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who fund the forgiven loan balances; the bill would also have rescinded unexpended appropriations from prior PSLF relief funds and shifted them into the rewritten program [S3]. Loan servicers and guaranty agencies would face new duties to supply repayment histories and issue notices.

drawbacks.text: The expanded program costs federal money: forgiving 50% of balances at five years and pulling FFEL borrowers into the program would increase the amount of debt the Treasury cancels, a cost an honest supporter has to weigh against the program's purpose [S3].

The bill effectively replaces the limited 'special PSLF' funds Congress appropriated in 2018 and 2019 by rescinding unexpended amounts, converting a capped temporary relief program into the broader permanent program [S3].

Defining qualifying employers broadly (including not-for-profits providing emergency, health, education, and legal services) and allowing payment 'buy-backs' for past periods adds administrative complexity for the Education Department and servicers, which is the kind of complexity that contributed to the original program's high denial rates [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for public service workers are large and concrete: faster forgiveness, access for previously excluded FFEL borrowers, and fixes to consolidation and notice rules that had caused many denials. The cost is real but targeted—additional loan cancellation borne by the federal government. The main design risk is administrative: the bill's fixes depend on the Education Department executing a complicated set of calculations and notices correctly, which the original program's track record gave reason to doubt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. John Sarbanes and Rep. Mark DeSaulnier introduced the bill on May 1, 2019 [S1, S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
Eighty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record [S4].
The bill's action history shows no further action—no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote—before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and the status quo: no expanded loan cancellation costs were incurred, and loan servicers and guaranty agencies avoided the new data and notice duties. Public service borrowers, who under the existing program continued to face high denial rates and ten-year waits, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and loan servicing status quo

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor

against.name: House Republican members of the Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Minority members of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no bipartisan base to press for action.

sides.party_line_note: All 82 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republicans on the bill; a Democratically-run committee nonetheless never acted on it, so the bill died without a recorded vote to split by party.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The bill imposes new duties on servicers, lenders, and guaranty agencies to provide repayment histories, participate in employment certification, and issue annual notices. It does not strip their servicing role, so their position in the system stays intact while their workload grows.

The expanded forgiveness (50% cancellation at five years, FFEL eligibility, retroactive relief) increases the loan balances the federal government cancels. For a public program aimed at public service workers, that cost is the bill's purpose rather than a side effect.

industries.industry: Public service employers (government, nonprofits, schools, hospitals)
industries.note: A faster, more predictable forgiveness program makes public service jobs more financially viable, helping governments and nonprofits recruit and retain teachers, nurses, and first responders. The bill's database of qualifying employers also lowers their certification paperwork.
